title: New Report Opens the 'Black Box' of Fertility Culture
gist: Executive-summary adaptation of the IFS/Wheatley 'Baby Nudges' report: a 10,000-person multi-country survey finds friend and parent support, admired celebrities, personal joy in children, risk tolerance and active faith predict fertility, while moral-obligation norms and chore division do not.

insights.claim: Fertility differs sharply among groups in the same economic setting: Ultra-Orthodox Jews in the New York metro averaged 7.5 children per woman from 2010 to 2026, versus 1.58 for college-educated native-born non-Hispanic white women, and Ohio Amish about 6 versus Ohio below 2.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Material factors alone cannot explain fertility gaps; culture is a distinct variable to model.

insights.claim: Treating culture as a residual catch-all for unexplained fertility variation obscures more than it illuminates, so the IFS/Wheatley report surveyed nearly 10,000 people in over a dozen countries and built an elite family-behavior database to identify specific cultural factors.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Marks a shift toward measurable cultural drivers of fertility in demographic research.
insights.quote: This “black box” approach to defining culture obscures more than it illuminates.
insights.locator: Unfortunately, “culture” has long been used as a catch-all term

insights.claim: Believing friends would celebrate a new baby is associated with a 10% higher desired number of children and 20% higher likelihood of intending another child, while parental encouragement is associated with 11% higher desired children and a 30% higher likelihood of intending another.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Social support and encouragement are quantifiable levers on fertility intentions.
insights.locator: Friends and family matter to fertility intentions.

insights.claim: Admiring a public figure with a family bigger than one's own is associated with a 14% higher likelihood of intending another child, and when low-fertility public figures capture more attention, fertility often falls.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Celebrity and media family norms may shape national fertility trends.
insights.locator: Admiring a public figure with a family bigger than one's own

insights.claim: Active faith matters for fertility, but the association is attributed to support from family and religious community members rather than the frequency of pro-family statements by religious leaders.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Community support, not clergy messaging, is the mechanism to watch.
insights.locator: Active faith matters to fertility desire and outcomes.

insights.claim: Belief in a moral obligation to have children does not significantly predict intending a child, whereas beliefs that children are the greatest joy or the future of one's community do.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Pronatal messaging should emphasize joy and community future, not duty.
insights.locator: Effective pronatal beliefs entail positive attitudes

insights.claim: Neither actual division of household chores nor perceived fairness significantly predicts fertility ideals or intentions, contrary to theories blaming unequal domestic labor for low fertility.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Chore-equity policy is unlikely to move birth rates.
insights.locator: Division of household labor does not have a big impact on fertility.

insights.claim: Willingness to take risks and optimism about the future predict fertility intentions and children born; safety-ism, general anxiety and pessimism are candidate drivers of falling fertility.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Rising anxiety is a possible cultural driver of the fertility decline; watch social-media and risk-hedging policy.
insights.locator: A willingness to take risks and an optimism about the future
